headline: Space budgets grow. Launch costs rise. Contracts multiply.
deck: This week saw increased funding for space resilience and a significant boost in launch contract ceilings.

stories.head: Space Force triples launch contract ceiling to $17B
stories.body: In a notable shift, the Space Force has tripled its launch contract ceiling from $5.6 billion to $17 billion, reflecting the growing demand for space access. This increase may be a response to the escalating costs associated with space operations, as the military acknowledges that the price of entry is only going up. Expect contractors to line up for a piece of this expanded pie.
stories.soWhat: This move suggests the Space Force is finally recognizing that space isn't a discount store.

stories.head: Pentagon invests $7.1M in satellite cover glass
stories.body: The Pentagon has allocated $7.1 million to enhance U.S. production of radiation-resistant cover glass for satellites. This investment underlines the importance of protecting assets in increasingly contested orbits, where a shiny finish could be the least of a satellite's worries. With rising tensions in space, even the glass is getting a military upgrade.
stories.soWhat: It’s a good reminder that even in space, aesthetics can’t overshadow functionality.

stories.head: Skyroot Aerospace achieves orbit with Vikram-1
stories.body: Skyroot Aerospace has successfully reached orbit with its Vikram-1 rocket on its first launch, marking a significant milestone for India's burgeoning commercial space sector. This achievement not only showcases India's growing capabilities but also positions Skyroot as a serious player in the global launch market. They may have just opened the floodgates for more Indian startups to follow suit.
stories.soWhat: Skyroot's success could mean a new wave of competition for established players like SpaceX and Rocket Lab.

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on the Artemis Accords
watchlist.body: With Mauritius signing on, the Accords could see more nations eager to join, expanding international collaboration in space.

watchlist.title: True Anomaly's Series C implications
watchlist.body: Their $190M raise indicates a strong push for co-orbital security, which could reshape the market dynamics for satellite defense.

watchlist.title: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser developments
watchlist.body: After passing its critical design review, the Dream Chaser could soon be a viable alternative in the cargo transport sector, if it ever actually launches.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN program extension
watchlist.body: The $480 million extension highlights the Pentagon's ongoing data obsession, which may lead to further investments in data-centric technologies.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
